When I first heard this game was "Slay the Spire hockey" I thought that sounded odd.  But it works.  You play short sessions of hockey resembling the era of games like NHL '93.  As you progress along the map you earn trait upgrades for your players, talents you can assign them (e.g., throw your stick to knock out an opponent skater, fart to repel your opponents), and artifacts that give you various bonuses.  Take on the boss team at the end of the map, and if you win you advance to the next map.  Earn rubber to spend after your run on attributes, new players that can be on your team, and new skills, all to be used in future runs.

My one complaint would be that the game feels a bit short.  It is still in early access as of now, so I would hope at some point by official release there is an endless mode added, where the boss teams get progressively more difficult.

[h1] Tape to Tape [/h1]  

[h2] First Impressions [/h2]  
[i] Tape to Tape [/i] blends the nostalgia of 90s NHL games with roguelite mechanics for a fresh and exciting hockey experience. It’s silly, challenging, and endlessly replayable—perfect for quick runs or long gaming sessions.

[h2] Pros [/h2]  
[list]  
    [*][b]Humorous and intuitive gameplay:[/b] Easy to learn, fun to master, with plenty of laughs along the way.  
    [*][b]Team creator:[/b] Build your custom squad and take them through the roguelike campaign.  
    [*][b]Outstanding developer support:[/b] Devs are incredibly responsive and actively engage with players.  
    [*][b]Great performance on Steam Deck:[/b] Smooth gameplay with only minor screen cut-off issues.  
    [*][b]High replayability:[/b] Each run feels unique, with varied skills and strategies to explore.  
[/list]

[h2] Grain of Salt [/h2]  
[list]  
    [*][b]Early Access quirks:[/b] Campaign acts and powers can feel unbalanced, and there are occasional graphical bugs.  
    [*][b]Future features pending:[/b] Exciting roadmap, including a season mode, but some features aren’t here yet.  
[/list]  

[h2] The Verdict: 9/10 [/h2]  
[i] Tape to Tape [/i] is a must-play for both hockey fans and roguelite enthusiasts. With its unique blend of sports and strategy, plus a passionate dev team delivering steady updates, this game is shaping up to be a full-course hockey feast. Get it now and join the action!

Gameplay & Mechanics:
Tape to Tape offers a smooth learning curve with fast-paced gameplay that keeps you engaged from the first faceoff. The controls are intuitive, making it easy for newcomers to pick up and play, while the moment-to-moment decisions add a satisfying layer of depth. The roguelite structure — with choices that carry real consequences — introduces meaningful risk and reward throughout each run. Whether you’re deciding which player to recruit or whether to bribe a referee, your decisions matter. The game avoids cheesy, overpowered combos, which helps maintain a fair and balanced feel across multiple playthroughs.

Visuals & Presentation:
The art style is cartoony without being childish, striking a fun yet polished tone. The visuals are clean and vibrant, helping the game stand out among sports titles. From menus to rink-side animations, everything has a slick, cohesive look that fits the game’s quirky charm without overwhelming the gameplay.

If you’re after a sports title that dares to be different, this one’s worth checking out.

Update: After communicating with the dev I think the game genuinely deserves playing, despite my initial issues and misgivings. Long review ahead, but bear in mind that these issues aren't common and likely had something to do with proton file corruption rather than the game itself.  

Tl;dr - Had some crazy technical issues, some nasty responses through steam comments from randos, finally found resolution, and got to genuinely try the game. 

################################################## 

It has been quite the journey, but I finally got this game working as intended on my deck. This review was initially negative, and I wish I could give it a mixed review as I am still not sold entirely. I had a lot of issues with this game on both an LCD and an OLED deck. I also had a friend with the same issue.

Troubleshooting steps consisted of the following before my previous negative review:

-Restarting deck
-Re-installing game 3 times.
-Moving game files from SD card to SSD and back, while trying it on both.
-Verifying local files twice.
-Trying multiple versions of proton (more on this later).
-Checking discord, reddit, steam forums for ideas (No sign of my problem).

As a side note, my decks are stock software. My LCD model had a screen I replaced due to an accident, and an upgraded SSD for increased storage space. My OLED has never been altered through hardware or software. My friend had a stock OLED as well. No tools, no home-brew, no Plug-ins, no anything (I was accused of this multiple times by game supporters). 

Comments on my initial review were derogatory and rude, though this doesn't represent the commmmunity as a whole. Ranging from how stupid I was to how I couldn't troubleshoot, and how I must have plugins installed that were interfering. I deleted unhelpful comments and the same people repeatedly commented, despite me explicitly detailing my troubleshooting attempts. I eventually turned off comments, but will turn them back on with this update. I didn't want to give up on a game I paid good money for so I continued to troubleshoot it. 

Now for the solution. I loaded the 5 latest protons, as well as GE and Proton experimental. Same issues I initially had were repeatedly encountered. I deleted my local proton files, and went through the above proton builds individually again. As I tried one, I would then delete the files, and try the next one. When I got to Proton 8.0-5 for the third time, the game miraculously started working. I tried this on my other deck with success. 8.0-5 didn't work initially, but worked after trying another version, deleting those proton files, then trying 8.0 again. 

The issues I had consisted of:
-Black screen on launch, intermittent.
-Early access banner blocking main screen on launch, and inability to close it, 6 launches in a row.
-When entering campaign, play button couldn't be activated. Shop could but the game would freeze immediately, requiring restart. This issue was consistent. 
-Black screen when starting a quick match, intermittent.
-Controls going completely unresponsive mid game, intermittent. 

I haven't had sufficient testing time, but after loading and closing the game multiple times, post solution I posted, I have encountered none of these. 

Finally, the games content. It is decent. The graphics are stylized so they will essentially be timeless. The game-play is unique and interesting. However, enemy AI and abilities are over-tuned while your team kind of sucks. I will caveat this by saying I am just now getting to properly play the game so this issue may be minor. 

Overall, it's an almost enthusiastic 1 thumb up from me. The game needs some work, and the issues were annoying, but the dev seems to genuinely care and be making honest effort. There is nothing else like it on the market though and it deserves a try if you like hockey or roguelites. It has hints of the old NBA Jam and backyard sports games from my childhood. Good luck, hopefully you are one of the lucky many that has no issues. If you aren't then maybe my solution can help you.

TL;DR/ Conclusion: The game is fun, charming, isn't expensive and is from a developer who cares and strives. Even if you get 10 hours out of it, it isn't a bad deal. Some might get 50 hours out of it in the current state. Please take my criticism below with a grain of salt and remember that the game is still in early access.

After 5 hours of game time, and about 3-4 runs, I beat the campaign on normal. It does seem a bit short and I'd love to see a bit more content added to the game.

When that is said, I think it's an incredibly satisfying game to play. First time starting the game, it felt so nice to skate around and pass the puck, to the degree I wished it was just a normal hockey game with more emphasis on the mechanics that already felt great to its core. There are a lot of rogue-lites out there lately, and I play a lot of them, that's why I wish it was not following the same formula.

But before you know it, You get that sense of satisfaction that those games give you. The feeling of OP abilities, upgrading our character, buying new superheroes in the store and all that good stuff. It's just a cozy game, not a try-hard/ super tactical game. Most of the fun comes from just trying out different things, enjoying the hillarious art style and either doing permant upgrades or upgrades within each run.

I'll play this game more before the full release, just to chill. It isn't really the game I want to play with a great challenge. That's why I'll wait with hard mode.

Nitpicking/ tips for the developers:

- The difficulty level of a run goes from extremely easy to pretty hard fast. Mostly because one playthrough is so short. I'd love to feel more invested in each run and to see the gradual development of my crew as well as the enemies. Right now, it can feel like all of a sudden I got completely OP or that the enemy got completely OP.

- Tuning down the power of each roguelite element. Some of the abilities we can use are quite OP and become the thing we lean on to win. Maybe I'm wrong about the enemies since I got better at understanding them and therefore beat the game, but it feels a bit like their unique powers are too overwhelming. This is just my opinion: maybe they should have higher base stats but lower boosts to their powers. The little prince can have less accuracy or shot power, the freeze that one team has can have reduced duration. Or else I at least feel that I am playing against only that power and not a complete team. It could be that this is solved in hard mode if the powers are still the same but base stats are increased. Can someone confirm?

- Currently, the 3 players who aren't your main character or superhero (they're called benchwarmers, right?) aren't good enough for me to want to give them the puck. The game revolves too much around the two stars of the team. It's not very out of balance and yes, they do bodycheck and score from time to time. I just miss the feeling of a fully coherent balanced team in a way. To be fair though, this will get better once my main character is fully upgraded so that upgrades during each run can be distibuted more to benchwarmers. I don't really want a team full of unique powers either since it will be a lot to try to remember while the game is already fast paced. Just a bit higher base stats would solve this for me.

- I want more customizeability for my team. I'd like to first of all be able to choose how my main character looks, choose team logo and colors. I also want to be able to buy players like benchwarmers, either permanently or maybe better just within each run. But since there's no currency within the runs, this might be a bad idea. You probably already have the best choice the way it is now.

- When I went into settings to rebind my gamepad controls, the first screen shows me keyboard. I started pressing the D-pad where I thought I had to go but it got stuck somewhere and I couldn't press anything. I had to restart the game. It feels a bit clunky to do the right thing. It did work the second time, but still, it was a long way up to "gamepad" at the top. No big deal, very much nitpicking.

- Each act is a long flat field. I'd love to see it as a mountain instead with each parts of the mountain changing based on the enemy. It would feel so epic. The terrain would be more interesting to look at and I'd get the feeling of climbing a ladder. Flat is just a bit boring. Also just nitpicking.

- Please be aware that I might not be right about anything I write here as feedback. It's more of a philosophical view that I wish I could play a long playthrough (let's say a season of 20 matches + cup matches or something) where the development and progression feels slower, yet more balanced. To reduce the chances of getting shocked because you got OP all of a sudden or getting absolutely crushed after an easy win before. It would also help me feel more invested in the game. In a longer season, it could be nice to have powers for the manager, or a unique button for a power done by an insider in the stands or on the bench. With this idea, I would still like that you keep the increase in difficulty from the enemies. It wouldn't make sense to be too weak early and too strong late compared to the opponents. As I'm writing this, I am not sure it would work at all because games that scale with you aren't really fun either. Rogue-lites aren't supposed to last long each run either. The way you give the player a chance to become OP is what makes a good rogue-lite. I just kinda miss a longer gameplay loop to feel more invested, that's all.

Once again, as I'm writing I'm coming up with a better approach to my idea here. Just please give us season mode without barely any upgrades or rogue-lite elements. Just give us the chance to buy new players, go up in tiers after winning the league, add more generic (less interesting) teams to fill up spots. Less focus on powers and humor, but more about the conquering of a league table and forming your entire team. Many sports games have different modes such as: manager mode, season mode, quick match. You have the perfect thing as a foundation which is the awesome rogue-lite game mode with really great mechanics. I want to complete every single mode you add. Variation is healthy and would make the game feel feature-rich.

So.. I do recommended this game it does come with a slight warning - I do like this game, I had fun playing this game, I would say if you're one of the 5 people in the world who've been demanding more Ice Hockey games release on PC it's definitely one to buy. 

However, I do think this game has a serious Achilles heel that cannot be ignored and is holding the game back in a bad way: No Career/Franchise Mode.

Despite the game having great graphics, great physics, great gameplay and overall being very fun... it's painfully short, with those 2.8 hours on record I have already beaten the final team and 'completed the game'. I find the refusal to include a Franchise Mode baffling, especially for a Singleplayer only game.

I want to get hooked and go deep into seasons building a team or player, recruiting talent, watching them grow, dealing with the finances, having rival teams, or creating my own character starting as a young talent with potential and levelling them up over the seasons - it's the only reason I play sports games when I play those Offline but I cannot do that here and I feel that it's holding this game back.

It's fun and it's worth the money especially when it goes on sale, but I didn't hook me in for very long and I came away feeling very mixed - happy to have a good Ice Hockey game, frustrated that it doesn't fill the Career shaped hole EA Sports left when it became Console only.

The last hockey game to garner my attention for long stretches was a recent revisit to NHL Hitz 20-03. published by Midway and developed by Black Box in 2002 the game had a robust franchise mode where you leveled up your team of scrubs to eventually be Stanley Cup contenders. This captures a similar essence with some 16 Bit NHL on top. It is still early access so the only game modes are Play Now, Its Rogue Lite Campaign, and Shootout as of this review, but the road map looks like it's shaping up to include more. It's about time someone picked up the mantle for a fun, over the top hockey game. While I'm not naive to the demand being low which is why many publishers have abandoned the concept this is clearly a labor of love for the sport and the genre. I wish nothing but the best for the devs. Keep up the good work, guys!

The concept is almost exactly where I've always wanted to see a sports game roguelite/RPG to be, but there's a lot of work that needs to be done on the gameplay loop and the flow.

A single loss can frustratingly put you out of a good run, which is something most roguelikes and roguelites generally avoid unless there's a significant payoff to the risk. An example would be an instant-death upgrade in a roguelite game until you "purify" it to receive a bonus to a stat.

Auto-changing characters is VERY frustrating, because there doesn't appear to be any rhyme or reason to what character is selected. I think this can be alleviated if I were to change characters with the right thumb stick? The problem though, is nearly every sports game out there offers auto-character selection that prefers near the puck, which has thus far not been my experience in the game.

The enemy goalie is MUCH better than mine. I'm not sure if this is balance-based, but I know it's not skill as the sheer number of shots I take to goals is much larger than the computer. We're talking like 25 to 1 versus 8 to 2. Even if they were all trash shots on my part, that's kind of bizarre.

It'd be nice to see the AI teammates doing a bit more. Right now they may occasionally throw a check out there, but that's pretty much it. They also have a terrible habit where ALL OF THEM of migrate to the side of the rink I'm on, providing me with no one to pass to for a backdoor shot.

The game seems to favor wholesale stat increases for the "non-all stars" much more than the all stars, but there's not much to do with that unless you're controlling said non-all star--which I do, because they, again, often have far better stats in the late game.

Early access though, so I imagine a lot of the kinks will be worked out, and anything that isn't may just be a problem I see that others don't. It's fun, but not a lot of replay value at the moment. It'd be cool to see a franchise mode or something.

My one complaint is the Bots in the campaign/quick play. The harder difficulties just feel cheap to play against because it just makes it unfair rather than more skillful. You can out-shoot the computer 60-5 but 4 of the 5 shots from the CPU went in despite your best attempts at defense, meanwhile the CPU goalie is making insane saves on every shot you attempt. Also playing single player, you can only control one player at a time, and your other skaters that are controlled by the CPU seem to also get dumber as difficulty goes up. So then it feels like a 5v1 where you're trying to manage your subpar CPU teammates. I'm all for a challenge at higher difficulty but doing it this way feels frustrating and unrewarding. 

A smaller thing that isn't really a complaint but rather something i noticed is that the game doesn't have any Offsides rules baked into it, so sometimes the CPU just sits a defender back in the O zone and lobs pucks to him and it'll screw you over if you're not paying attention. 

Overall I'd recommend this game if you do like hockey or arcade sports games. I'm going to keep playing it despite the small flaws

I've been looking for an NHL Hitz-style game for what seems like forever, but everything I've played has fallen short. One problem this game has (like literally every other hockey game in history) is cheap goals. Far too many times is the cpu opponent able to seemingly score at will. It forces you to place as tight defensively as possible, which, to an extent, is good, it just shouldn't be because the cpu can score from anywhere on the ice whenever it wants or is needed. It's a gripe I would have with any game, so it's not unique to Tape to Tape.

The customization of uniforms is nice, but quickly falls flat when you realize it's only one template that you get to recolor, rather than having a variety of designs and styles. It's something that could possibly be added in the future, which I hope is the case.

I've seen the development road map for the game and it looks like there will eventually be a season mode. That's great, but how about a franchise mode? How about a bit of depth? How about significantly expanded customization for both uniforms and created players? These are all things I'd love to see.

Tape to Tape has the potential to be a game that becomes a cult classic, something people look back on and say, "Yeah, I miss playing that game, it was so much fun," but in order to get there, there needs to be a lot more content and a lot more options and functionality. Definitely a great place to start, though. Fingers crossed.

Tape to Tape is a refreshingly bold and stylized take on ice hockey that brings arcade energy and roguelite progression to a sport rarely explored in the indie gaming space. Developed by Excellent Rectangle, this title strikes a clever balance between fast-paced, skill-driven gameplay and tongue-in-cheek charm, offering a sports experience that feels both nostalgic and inventive. At its core, Tape to Tape is not just about scoring goals—it’s about building a team, overcoming unpredictable challenges, and mastering a fluid, physics-based system that rewards precision and adaptation. Whether you're a die-hard hockey fan or someone drawn in by the unique aesthetic and mechanics, the game makes a strong case for itself.

The most striking aspect of Tape to Tape is its roguelite structure. Unlike traditional sports titles that focus on full-season simulations or career modes, this game drops players into a randomized campaign where each run is a new journey. You start with a modest team and face off against increasingly difficult opponents, collecting upgrades, recruiting better teammates, and picking passive or active abilities that can drastically alter your style of play. This structure adds a layer of strategic decision-making between matches, where you’re constantly thinking not just about the next game, but how your choices will affect the overall run. The sense of progression is meaningful, and even in defeat, there’s often a takeaway that makes the next run feel fresh and more promising.

Gameplay is fast, fluid, and deceptively deep. The controls are intuitive enough for newcomers to pick up quickly, yet the underlying mechanics allow for a lot of finesse. Tape to Tape encourages creativity on the ice—passes, checks, dekes, and shots all feel dynamic thanks to the physics-based engine. It’s not just about stats or brute force; timing, spacing, and smart use of special abilities can turn the tide of a game in seconds. Each character brings unique strengths, whether it’s a speedy skater, a heavy hitter, or a goalie with clutch-saving reflexes. The AI is competent enough to provide a challenge, especially in later runs, and the boss matches—larger-than-life showdowns with quirky, themed teams—are highlights that break up the rhythm and inject humor into the grind.

Stylistically, Tape to Tape adopts a vibrant, hand-drawn art direction that sets it apart from more sterile or hyper-realistic sports games. Characters are cartoonish, expressive, and full of personality. Animations are smooth and exaggerated in a way that leans into the arcade feel without sacrificing clarity or control. The arenas are equally stylized, sometimes featuring bizarre obstacles or environmental twists that enhance the game’s offbeat tone. This aesthetic approach pairs perfectly with the game’s irreverent humor—team names, dialogue, and events are often packed with puns, references, or absurd scenarios that give the game a distinct voice and keep things lighthearted.

Multiplayer is also well-handled, with both local and online options that let you test your skills against friends or strangers. While the roguelite campaign is the star, competitive modes provide longevity and replay value beyond the single-player runs. Playing against others adds another layer of unpredictability, and the quick match format makes it ideal for casual sessions or more intense rematches. The game continues to receive updates, with the developers actively refining balance and adding new content, which helps the overall package feel alive and supported.

That said, Tape to Tape isn’t without its flaws. Because of its roguelite design, there can be occasional pacing issues—particularly if you hit a bad streak of random events or upgrades. The difficulty curve can also spike sharply depending on matchups and RNG, which may frustrate some players who prefer more consistency in their progression. Additionally, while the mechanics are fun, the relatively small pool of abilities and players can start to feel repetitive after extended play. However, these are issues that may be addressed with future updates, and even in its current form, the gameplay loop is compelling enough to keep you coming back.

Overall, Tape to Tape is a highly original and entertaining fusion of arcade sports action and roguelite design, breathing new life into the hockey genre with style, humor, and heart. Its emphasis on tight controls, strategic upgrades, and unpredictable match scenarios makes every run a new challenge, while the expressive visuals and quirky presentation give it a charm all its own. It’s not just a sports game—it’s a roguelite adventure on ice, and one that’s easy to recommend to anyone looking for something different, fun, and surprisingly deep. Whether you’re chasing a championship or just looking to land the perfect slapshot, Tape to Tape delivers a uniquely satisfying hockey experience.

With all the roguelite power-ups, luck feels more important than skill, which can lead to some frustration. I found the Easy difficulty to be too easy, while Standard felt cheap.

The early access version of the game is also quite short and low on game modes. That said, if you go into it with the mindset this is an indie sports game with some new ideas, I feel like it's worth the relatively low price of admission. Whether it eventually evolves to something greater remains to be seen, but I'm glad there are people still making sports games with original ideas.

If you like hockey and are looking for a game that you can play whenever with little time commitment, other than initially getting used to the controls, then this is worth exploring. Fast paced, rougelite, challenges, and no two games or teams are ever the same. Win or lose a run, you're excited to see what crazy combos you can craft when designing your team. The fact that the power ups that you can select differ from run to run also make your decisions a little tricky based on how you like the play. 

Things to note and consider before buying: 

1. Early game is painful. Figuring out the play style, the strengths of opposing teams, and building up enough currency to buy power ups can and will be frustrating. As will be the first time you play the first boss. If you can accept this and just keep trying, it'll be rewarding. 

2. If you're a hockey purist, know that a lot of that's out the window here. While good hockey sense, like cycling, centering, etc is still all valuable, there isn't things like offsides or icings. (Usually...) So you have to get used to that. Additionally, you'll need to allow yourself to be okay with the power ups. The first time you make the perfect cross ice pass only to have the opposing goalie fart and blow the puck behind your player ready to bury the shot top shelf will enrage you. But it's all about adjusting your playstyle to address each new team. 

2.5 But the first time you put a curve ball shot skill on your winger, and they score from the blue line, you'll be so happy...so it does go both ways. 

3. If you don't have a controller, playing on a keyboard will take time getting used to. 

4. Number 3 again, but double it for being able to change to the player you want. If you're trying to defend a breakaway and you'd think the player you get control of is the one closest the puck...you'll sometimes be wrong. Weird event happens that just leaves the puck by itself in front of the other team's goal, and your sniper is streaking toward the puck and you want to change to them? ...Sometimes you'll pick up your defender. You can still beat the campaign, but knowing this happens ahead of time is helpful. 

If you can be okay with all of that, then you still have a fun and goofy game to enjoy. It's nice because if you have twenty minutes to kill, and the thought of loading up a game that you can't just save at any point and you don't have the emotional energy for, is a lot, then Tape to Tape is the perfect game to just have some fun.

In current state of game's early access, the campaign is a series of 5v5 hockey games where you play against a variety of wacky teams. Successful runs on normal take maybe 1-1.5 hours, with individual games going as short as 30 seconds but usually less than 5 minutes.

As of this writing I got ~20 hours out of it and feel satisfied with the available experience, and am excited to see what comes as EA progresses.


----------------------------
Unsolicited feedback time:

I said the game is 5v5, but most of the time it feels like 1v10; me vs the 5 opponents, my 4 teammates, and the controls of the game itself. At first, this was EXTREMELY frustrating, but then I kind of came to enjoy figuring out how to play around my teammates refusing to position themselves in ways that make sense. Remember playing hockey/soccer as a kid and how everyone just clumps up around the puck/ball? Yep. Frustrating because the most effective way to score is one-timers (20 hours in and I'm really not sure if it's possible to score with pure slapshots), but teammates will rarely position themselves to take advantage. Also the 10th opponent, the controls, frequently enjoys passing to teammates who have no business being a valid target for the pass. Sometimes I'll be putting up goals one after another effortlessly, and sometimes I feel like the game is purposefully pumping the opponent goalie with OVR so I can never possibly score. I know the programming the logic for each player and the various physics isn't easy at all so I'm willing to forgive the current system quite a bit and I'd wager this is where most dev time goes, still gonna throw my voice out there.

The RPG elements are frankly criminal. Having to spend rubber on Angus getting better might make sense from perspective of 'people get better at things over time', but this is a video game where things get absurd quick and then magically return to status quo. It feels like I'm intended to have artificially worse experiences early on for the sake of inflating gameplay time. The game is fun, you don't need to do that. Remove this, give Angus static stats that can be improved/changed during a run.

Speaking of, the hockey blacksmith is a very funny hook right from the menu, but is wasted on a lame metaprogression shop. Why is he not appearing during the run? Forget the Rest areas on the map, that should be hockey blacksmith forging better gear to increase stats/equipment. Meta shop should be saved for more interesting meta elements, see the mirror in Hades
as an example. The power to reverse a goal once would make sense as a meta option, similar to Death's Defiance. Just spitballing, current system is joysucking. 

The map in general could be made more interesting. As is, I don't know why anyone would willingly go to rests/events over games for talents when given the choice. Some events are actually curses, and some are good but have obvious options. With the bonus to OVR during a period, why would anyone not take +50 OVR in the first perior? Thanks to the mercy mechanic it's the only option that makes sense. Then for the bad events, you can skip but you still lost a talent by not choosing the correct option in the first place. Would really benefit from copying Slay the Spire's homework a bit more: a 3 pronged map at all times, not being forced into the current pattern of talent, rest, full game, talent, full game, boss. Let me choose between elite games for talents/artifacts, playing it safe if things aren't looking hot, or training/blacksmithing. Let me recruit and swap in new players and switch gear around after the fact. There's already a gear system, and a blacksmith! Lean more into sportsy-ness and let me modify my team a bit more.

I get the game is a delicate balance between keeping it grounded enough to still be an accessible sports game, and full on video gamey roguelike wackiness. Personally, I would enjoy leaning muuuuch further into roguelike wackiness. Longer runs, weirder powers, weirder and more varied opponents. Wouldn't even mind if runs were significantly longer. Putting it out there.

All that said, I got 20 hours of enjoyment current state and eagerly await more so all these criticisms are from a place of really liking the game and hoping it achieves greatness and gets more attention.

Having nearly 150 hours into this thing, I have some thoughts that I think are worth sharing.

Pros
- The general flow of a run is absolutely fantastic. You can get pretty crazy with some combos and abilities that you earn, especially by the third leg of an attempt. 
- Core hockey is generally great, and the foundation is here for something special should they choose to keep improving on things
- The different teams are all fairly unique and fun, with the exception of the meatball team in the first leg (I can't remember the last time I DIDN'T mercy them). And the Greasy Lettuce could use some buffs, but are closer to the latter half of the special teams than the meatballs.
- The great abilities are truly wonderful to play with. My personal favorite has to be the Dash, since it opens up all sorts of wild possibilities when combined with other powers. 
- The various superstars that you unlock are the best part of the entire game in my opinion. That kazoo, though. Too tasty!
- The overall visual style is consistent, fun, and effective. I like the direction they chose, and look forward to more wacky creations from them in the future
- The UI is clean, clear, and does its job. The main menus are snappy and responsive. One of the cleaner early access games I have played in terms of how sharp it is.
- Have never run into any game breaking bugs, with just some minor annoyances here and there like weird audio problems that they are aware of.
- For the most part (more on this in the Cons), the difficulty curve is satisfying and generally satisfying. Winning a run against those Golfers is delicious beyond words.

Cons
- Holy hell the passing in this game is so bad sometimes. It doesn't need a complete overhaul, but it's close. I would say 40% of my passes go not only to the wrong person, but to the WORST POSSIBLE person on my team. It is the single biggest drawback for me at the moment and needs addressed in a huge way.
- The goalies are better with the latest patch, but still need some tweaking. I can score almost 100% of the time by just rushing past them with Dash, and that shouldn't happen.
- The Princesses are absurd. As a person who has pulled off a mercy on the Golfers, I can safely say the Princesses are straight up broken. They have the fart (incredibly powerful, albeit funny, ability), sticks to throw at you, insane speed, accuracy, and buckwild checking power. If they were a freakin boss they would be too good in my opinion. Of all content in the game that needs a nerf, they win that award by about 1,000% for me
- Some abilities just straight up suck in my opinion. The whirlwind is bad, and the dragon shout is a neat idea but is just a Disco Ball with a different name and longer cooldown. 
- Goalies make the dumbest passing choices, and sometimes they don't even respond correctly. If I am pressing up/right towards my only guy on screen...why is my goalie passing down/right to the point that the puck is mere inches away from going into the goal? 
- We need a better way to switch players. Let me assign hotkeys to everyone on my team, or stop thinking I want to choose the slowest player that is furthest from the puck instead of the fastest player that is closest to the puck. Please for the love of god lol
- There needs to be a teammate AI basic script we can choose. I want my players to become aggressive or focus on checking or racing after the puck instead of going into canned movement animations when they are on "offense" or "defense." 
- The point above is painfully apparent when facing the Prince. The only reason he is even a threat is because your team doesn't even try to check him, and it's a dumb way to increase the difficulty. They need to let your team check on their own and just cut his wind up speed in half. It would feel less cheap while retaining the flavor of what they intended him to be in the first place

Overall the game is absolutely fantastic, and for being in early access I don't think any of the Cons are unreasonable to be present in the product. Making games is hard, and they are clearly taking their time to make this one correctly. Even if all my gripes go unanswered because they consider other feedback more valuable, I will keep playing it for as long as they keep releasing new content for it.

This game combines the feel of classic arcade style sports games (think NFL Blitz, NBA Jam, Backyard Sports, etc.) with a rogue-like campaign format.  Overall the gameplay is solid with simple, intuitive, and responsive controls.  There is just enough realistic physics to make it feel like a hockey game (players can't turn 180 degrees without losing speed/momentum, for example), but otherwise the game is loaded with arcade-y shenanigans that keep things silly and lighthearted.

As the game truly is a melding of two design philosophies (arcade sports and rogue-like), I will judge each separately.

Arcade Hockey Elements:  8.5/10
The controls are easy to pick up and understand, making it accessible to experienced gamers and newcomers alike.  There are no penalties and no offsides rules in the game, so the action keeps moving.  Hockey staples like one-timers and net-front tips are included seamlessly, with the latter happening automatically if the player is in front of the net.  Body checking is generally very effective at knocking a player off the puck, or knocking a player down before the puck gets to them (remember, no penalties).  Players will also stick check automatically if they are close enough to their opponent, so you don't have to rely solely on smashing into your opponents to get possession.

The hockey experience falls just short of 10 due primarily to the AI.  The computer opponent generally has good positioning fundamentals, with certain opponents being more or less aggressive in the campaign mode, forcing you to adjust your strategy.  However, your own AI teammates often make baffling decisions.  Sometimes one or two of them will skate right next to you when you are carrying the puck, getting in your way and also blocking you from making other passes, as they will catch any pass you try to make to teammates beyond them.  They will also frequently overskate the net, taking themselves out of the play and missing out on otherwise golden rebound shot attempts (the opponent AI seems to do this far less frequently).  Finally, the goalie has some sort of bug that makes his passes erratic.  Sometimes he will pass the puck where you indicate, and sometimes he will pass the puck in a random direction (though this appears to affect the computer opponent as well).

Rogue-like elements:  7/10
There are a lot of fun and creative ideas here.  Players have stats that you can increase, and you can gain passive and active talents for players throughout the campaign.  Some of them are far more useful than others, however, with certain talents backfiring on you more often than not.  During the campaign, your opponents scale in difficulty, with each boss and mini-boss having their own talents and abilities that you have to overcome.  Some of these can be quite frustrating to play against, particularly the Act 2 and Act 3 bosses, who both have abilities and rink modifiers that fundamentally change the game, making it feel a little less like an arcade hockey game.  This element of the game loses some points in my evaluation as in these cases the gameplay crosses the line from challenging into frustrating a bit more often than I would like.

Overall this game is at least an 8/10, and well worth the price they are asking.  There is a lot of charm and polish to the game that I haven't listed above (my review would be pages long if I did).  I would recommend the game to anyone who is looking for an arcade-style hockey game, and anyone who enjoys rogue elements and sports games in general.  If you are easily frustrated by rogue-style games where sometimes you just get dealt bad luck, or if you get frustrated by the simplicity and silliness that can accompany arcade-style games, this may not be for you.

Are you looking for a fun yet not too serious hockey game? Tired of playing hockey games that overcomplicate everything, and want to sit back and enjoy a unique hockey gaming experience? Looking for an entertaining hockey game to play co-op or against your friends?

Tape to Tape is the game you’re looking for. Initially, I was impressed by how much fun this game is, especially when played with friends. You’ll never play the same hockey game twice, as it features roguelite elements with unique hockey players, abilities, and even arenas. I’ve never played a hockey video game where you can play a game on a soccer field using soccer balls without hockey sticks, or a golf ball on a golf course.

It’s a fantastic hockey game, and even though it’s in Early Access at the time of this Steam Review, there is more than enough to keep you busy. The campaign mode is incredible, and even after beating it multiple times, it never got boring, since you’ll always get random players and abilities on every run.

Much respect to the developer, Excellent Rectangle, for creating such a magnificent game so far and continuing to implement smart updates based on all our feedback. This is how it should be done, and once the game officially launches, it should perform well. The foundation is there, and if they can continue building upon it, this will be a must-play arcade hockey game.

That’s the beauty of keeping this game simple to play, but having a lot of depth in unique gameplay.

Throw in some great memories with friends in both co-op and versus, and you have the makings of a future hockey video game classic. If you love hockey as much as I do, buy this game. - Switching is TERRIBLE: Switching between players is haphazard and you never know what you're gonna get; do you want to switch to a specific player? Nah, the game pretty much decides which player you'll switch to.

- Inconsistent difficulty: Yes, this is a rogue-like, and on expert difficulty it's supposed to be hard. I get that. However, I can't help but to feel like the difficulty spikes are totally random - regardless of whether you face a boss or not.

- Lack of deking: No deking. At best, you'll wiggle your left thumbstick to fake the goalie out. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. 

Overall, there's much to be enjoyed (as my playtime might suggest) but if the above mentioned "problems" are either ironed out or at least tweaked, the game would be vastly superior.

Goals are scored almost exclusively by one-timer.  There's no strategy to speak of; every play is crash the net to set up a one-timer. - player-switching seems to be totally random. The first player you get is basically never the one in reach of the puck or the enemy puck-carrier. That's hell of annoying

The game engine and controls for this game are fantastic. This is a great hockey game engine and it's so nice to see a modernized version of old school console hockey.

The game is fairly unusual in design, in that it has superpower abilities that are sort of over the top in design, that allow you do things like ricochet the puck off off people's heads to knock them out or throw your stick like a tomahawk while having multiple hockey sticks strapped to your back as backup sticks. The game is also a roguelike game, which is actually a pretty cool idea where you keep trying to succeed at games until you lose, and then unlock different abilities and stats over time. Sounds good? There's one big problem: the rules of hockey were removed from the game. Big deal? Well, here's one example of a few problems:

The OFFSIDE rule doesn't exist in this game (where you can't pass the puck over the blue line of the opponent's zone if one of your teammates is already in the zone). This means any player (even the CPU goaltender, who will do this often) can flip the puck into the opponent's zone onto the stick of one of his teammates who is standing right next to the opponent's net, and then he'll have a free shot. There needs to be a defensive player dogging every opponent at all times because nothing is stopping them from standing a mile away from the action and waiting for the big lob pass across the arena that gives a free breakaway / slapshot into the net.

For the sake of not spoiling other surprise parts of the game, I won't go over all the different teams and the broken rules that get introduced and how they're abused, but this game essentially acts best as a reminder on why there are certain rules in hockey. The game design has taught me that hockey wouldn't become "more fun" if we took the rules away, with the experience being quite dull overall after playing a few games of such limited strategy.

With that said, the game has just released into early access, so there is still time for the design of the game to steer itself toward something more than an amazing hockey engine with wasted potential. I will change my review if the game manages to fix some of the oversights that rob the game of being enjoyable for me.

As a hockey (and hockey game) fan, like many others on PC, I've been craving a good hockey game to come back on the platform. Similar to Super Blood Hockey, I think this has some potential as an arcade-style hockey game, but it misses the mark on a few things that take away the enjoyment. As of now, I can't recommend the game in its current form.

The campaign is pretty frustrating in that as soon as you lose you get sent back to the beginning and only then can you upgrade your core player. I'm not sure if the bench players get upgraded as well, or if you can upgrade other stats - the game doesn't really make it clear. Why is the path through the campaign always the same? As a roguelite game, there should be some random paths implemented, different opponents added, and so on. In this game, it's always the same, which gets frustrating and boring very quickly. Adding different branches on a larger map, letting you participate in skills tournaments or other challenges on your way, might be a fun thing to do. For example, you might challenge some people on a pond hockey game with a different sized rink and some funky rules (no goalies, and only a small target to hit). Or there might be a skills competition, where you pick which events you participate in for a chance to improve a bunch of different attributes. Maybe with different branches, at the start of the campaign all the arenas and other locations are hidden from you, but over time you can upgrade your team's "scouting" abilities (maybe adding a coach attribute) and you can reveal what those paths have as achievable bonuses so you can better pick which path to go on. The way it is now though, you have very little choice in which path you go on, essentially being railroaded through the campaign... I hate facing the same opponents over and over again. 

Reaching checkpoints where you can visit the shop and not have to start all over again when you lose would be nice as well.

Another thing that is important to the game is... how do you score goals? In the practice mode, they don't explain it. They also don't teach you how to use each of the special abilities. How do I use the yo-yo effectively? It's not explained. Does deking or doing east-west passes for a one-timer actually improve your chances of scoring, or is it a dice-roll in the background? Is it better to just take a slapshot and rely on your player's power, or is it better to do a wrist shot and rely on accuracy? None of this is explained, and even someone like me - who is intimately familiar with hockey - can't really tell. I don't understand the point of the Tomahawk ability, either. Sure, you can drop one or two players in front of you with your stick, but usually the AI just takes the puck from you since you can't quickly switch to another player once your Tomahawk player has lost their stick. What's the point? If you added some practice for each skill, and showed us how to use each effectively, then it'd be much more useful. Also, as someone else said in their review, adding more abilities and making it a completely random selection just leaves me with a higher chance to get abilities I don't want at all... kind of defeats the purpose. 

Maybe I haven't gotten far enough in the game to know how to do this, or if it's possible, but I would've thought we should be able to swap out all our players for star players eventually, rather than just having one single star player on the team. Shouldn't that be the goal of this game, to eventually make a superstar team that goes all the way to a championship? If not then maybe there should be a Campaign+ mode where you can utilize all the unlocked players in your lineup and swap them out as the game progresses and unlock more. 

Your defense is basically useless. They don't knock players down, block passes, or perform takeaways. When you take over the nearest player, they don't seem to do anything while skating backwards, and the transition to skating forwards with the attacking player is too slow. The AI is always able to avoid me, or pass to an open player, 99% of the time. If there's a technique to this then put it in the practice/tutorial! Otherwise, you have to change it. The only technique I've found to make my defense somewhat effective is to give one of them the random ability to seek out the other team's players and bodycheck them, and then I always let the AI use that player since they seem to be way better at bodychecking the other AI than I am.

Not being able to upgrade your goalie seems like a significant oversight, as others have mentioned. Maybe getting a superstar goalie, or one who can better stop special abilities, would be a good addition.

All in all, the game started to scratch my itch for a simple hockey game that reminded me of the old SNES NHL 90-something games, but ultimately if there was a choice between playing them in an emulator on PC or playing Tape to Tape, I'd probably still choose the old NHL games. There are definitely ways to improve it, and I hope the Early Access will allow them to try some bold changes in the game behind the scenes and eventually give us a game that's both challenging and enjoyable.

I wish I could say that I liked this game. Hockey is a sport dying for some love on the PC, and this game is so incredibly charming, has a unique premise, and is clearly the passion project of an incredibly talented developer. But an arcadey sports game, first and foremost, should be fun to play and Tape to Tape just doesn't meet its potential. 

First, let me share everything I love about the game. The sprites and art direction of this game is incredible. It has an almost Saturday morning cartoon atmosphere with 8 direction player models that give off a faux 3D effect a la the PlayStation and Nintendo 64 era. This game is nice to look at and clearly a lot of effort went into its premise and character. This game has a lot of character. This game also runs really well on various PC hardware as well, which should be expected given the graphical fidelity of this game. 

From a controls perspective, the skating feels good enough for me, and the passing can be tweaked by forcing nearest passer if the pass assist isn't to your liking. The roguelike aspect is something I could see other sports games emulating in the future because it is a good idea. 

Again, Excellent Rectangle put a lot of effort into a unique experience that tried to offer something to hockey fans who are stuck on PC without a game to play that isn't NHL 2004. But on to what I didn't like

The novelty of the powerups and teams are funny to experience but does not give a great gameplay experience, and in general, games feel like a rubber bandy mess rather than a tight, pick-up-and-play game. Games can feel unfair regularly and I find myself just not being interested in continuing to play this game. 

The goaltending might be the most egregious part of the game. On harder difficulties it feels like you have a bantam goaltender while your computer opponent has the love child of Andrei Vasilevskiy and Dominik Hasek in net. I find myself getting pretty frustrated when I'm ahead on the shot total and my goaltender is a sieve just because I'm playing on hard. it's an illusion of difficulty which is created by making your computer teammates more inept, more prone to mistakes outside the player's control. I've only had goals in my own net on hard for example.

Ultimately, it's hard to recommend this game mainly due to its AI. A good hockey game fundamentally needs good AI, and even though I applaud this developer and am encouraging them to do more. This game just isn't good enough for me to recommend.

I've played enough hours now I feel I can give an informed review.

Good:

- The art style and game mechanics are fun and engaging, and hit the right spot of nostalgia for NHL '94 fans

- The gameplay is fast paced and rewards good puck control

- Passing and shooting feel solid

- It is the best PC hockey game in recent memory

Bad:

- Your players lose control of the puck way too easily. Expert mode is ridiculous to the point of being unfun.

- The AI routinely scores goals from distance on shots that land less than 1/50 times for a human player, and that is not an exaggeration. Be prepared to lose your entire run because of the terrible AI of your goalie, repeatedly.

- Playing defense feels too much like a roll of the dice because the game is terrible at figuring out which player you are trying to switch to on defense. You will often lose the game (and consequently your entire run) solely because of it. 

Suggestions to devs:

- Audience animations would add a lot of color to the mix 

- When you go to start a new game you only have the option to choose from one of three randomly selected star teammates. This only leads to me restarting if I don't get to select the one I just bought or actually want to use. I'm not sure what the point is of limiting the options.

- The main changes in Expert mode seem to be a) making it incredibly easy to lose control of the puck if an opponent gets even remotely close to you and b) severely nerfing your goalie, who will suddenly let in a lot of terrible shots from outside. There is not much the player can do to shore up these disadvantages, which makes the increase in difficulty feel cheap.

Overall, worth the price of admission even though it needs some tweaks and worth rewarding the devs for having the cojones to put out a good hockey game on PC. However the game's terrible goalie AI and inability to effectively switch which player you are controlling often results in a very frustrating experience, and none of the updates have addressed these issues.

Tape to Tape is a very unique game concept. As a sports fan I thought the concept of a Hockey Roguelite was worth going in blindly even though I am not a huge fan of Roguelites.

On the surface Tape to Tape is a fun little arcade hockey game that is a heavily arcade-fantasy style sports game. My personal opinion its leans too much arcade as there are literally no rules. No, icing, no off-sides, no penalties.

[b]NO OFF-SIDES.[/b] This is the biggest rule that really affects game play and strategy. After a few games you will quickly realize that off-sides in Hockey is a huge rule that adds strategy and makes the game more exciting because without it you can easily cherry pick and freely skate around the ice with the puck where ever you choose.

This one thing really soured me on the gameplay. Each match devolves into the same thing, w/o off-sides the core Hockey mechanics quickly became quit stale.

There are other minor rule issues that I can look past as an arcade hockey game but off-sides, nope.

The game features crazy reality breaking abilities like AOE farts that knock down players, throwing your stick at players to knock them down. Slapshots to the head that knock down players, freezing players in a block of ice for long periods of time.

Earlier where I said the game leans too far into the fantasy aspect, this is where it got crazy for me and not in a good way. I likes some of the stuff like throwing your stick. Once I got to the AOE fart abilities or the Ice Block or the Teleporting stuff I began to think how stupid and how unrelated this game was to actual hockey.

Its frustrating, I want to like this game but 3 hours of playing I came to the conclusion that the only thing I like about this game is that its Hockey related.

I got annoyed early on at the music and celebration animations. I came to hate the humor and art style and the "quirky" aspects of the game. 

The core gameplay is quite bare-bones once sink your teeth into it. No stick/poke check. No deke. Checking is very poorly animated and controlled, movement feels pretty bad. You can't control the goalie while in goal. You can't manually select a player while on the ice, you can just cycle through them or hope you select the guy closest to the puck. You can't dive or kneel to block, there is no block button. There is essentially only one kind of shot, no wrist-shots. Most goals will look the same, crash the net one timers.

I think the concept has some potential but the execution isn't there. I honestly think you may like this game more if you don't give a shit about hockey but if you LOVE hockey you will see all the flaws that pile up and make this game NOT hockey at all.

This game is Early Access, maybe they can improve over time but I would avoid for now.

The "roguelite" elements of it are very evidently a complete afterthought and were probably only tossed in in the last quarter of pre-release development. Your campaign protagonist and team start out generally useless, but even upgrading your protag's stats between runs and buying new abilities and this and that just do not feel that impactful. "Upgrades" very seldom feel like they actually do anything of value a lot of the time, especially when the AI doesn't tend to make many mistakes on account of being AI. They will see what you're trying to do and they will make the objectively correct play to counter it without fail, and a lot of the time that boils down to either being designed to have absurd stats in some category to brute force you or an ability that says "You are no longer allowed to play the game", or some mix of those.

The "Princess" team, despite overall being the second easiest team to beat after the Referee team from the end of the first act, is in my experience the absolute worst of the first two acts hands down. You will spend 95% of the game trying to make a play and having some ugly pink fatass FART on you and you just go flying to the other side of the ice, usually into one of their players who will check you. It's really just a reaction speed test to see if you can pass after seeing that FART CLOUD. Are we 10 years old again? Are fart jokes still funny?

Juvenile jokes aside, farting at the very least isn't one of the many AI abilities they aggressively use off cooldown to tell you "I hate you, fuck off and give me that puck. You aren't supposed to be playing", which is in my eyes one of the worst possible design choices they could have made. A million and one ways to say "Stop playing for a sec real quick, K?" with your biggest counter just being to aggressively pass between players and pray that there's no interception and that the guy you're passing to doesn't promptly eat shit too. Sure would be nice if you could buff defense too, instead of the asinine accuracy stat. But oh, I guess you can if you want to move at a snail's pace, which is genuinely just the worst choice you can make because you simply won't be able to apply enough pressure anymore to make up for the fact that:

Your goalie is a vegetable. A genuine vegetable. He will stand 8 feet out from his crease and just stare as the opposing team speeds towards him with the puck, making token gestures of resistance as they go around either of his sides and earn seemingly scripted goals. You let the other team take the puck to your goal, thus you are now on a timer to outdo them or restart. Sure would be nice if their goaltender seemingly never made the same mistakes yours did, more actively sticking opposing players and HUGGING that net like it was his momma. Ironically the most reliable way I've found to score isn't to shoot at all, but to stick my entire body into their goalie's arms and just -pass- the puck into their net right before he topples me like a jenga tower. I have no idea why that works, but the goalies seemingly have no idea how to deal with that and as such I try to make it a habit not to use it. 
Despite the game frequently telling me to stop playing.
But hey, I think I'm going to listen to the game. After nearly 2 hours of being told to stop playing? I think I'll do just that. Pass me that $20 back, devs. :)

This game will almost assuredly be a good game in about a year if the devs keep it up.  

However, my advice is let this one bake in the oven until then.  Even on sale, $18 is a big ask for a game that occasionally fundamentally is broken.  If that sounds harsh, just a reminder that this game is a single elimination (i.e. one loss and you restart) rogue-lite hockey game that has absolutely no rules whatsoever implemented currently other than one corrupt ref in one specific boss fight that will almost consistently call one of your (valid) goals off because the gimmick is that they are corrupt.

Every other match is a glorified tennis match due to no offsides or icing, and the best strategy is often to get the puck to one of your fastest mates and have them burn down the timer once you get a lead.  Alternatively, you can just position your best shooter offscreen by the enemies goal, and as soon as you get puck possession simply whip it up the ice towards your winger waiting for a free shot.  The CPU does this as well, and if you try to play normal regulation hockey you'll often get countered by the CPU exploiting the lack of rules.

Being hockey, losses can be subject to a random bounce.  This is why most regulation hockey has series, or best of 5/7/etc.  In Tape to Tape, that one lucky bounce can end your hours-long run.  

There's a lot to like about this, but it's gotta bake and work out the issues.

Save your money, wait for updates maybe? This doesn't play like a hockey game and is something else.

Love absolutely everything about this game…except for playing it. This should be my perfect game in theory. I love rougelikes and sports games with progression. The power ups are all super cool and I love the cast of characters. 

However, the second you hit the ice it all falls apart too much for me to recommend. Passes going to the wrong person constantly, or often times no one at all. Shots taken that end up parallel with the blue line instead of aimed at the net. 

From what I’ve been able to determine, the problem comes from using the same stick for movement as you do aiming your passes and shots. It makes it extremely difficult to move your character and pass or shoot at the same time. 

Don’t get me started on how inconsistent defense is. I can’t tell you how many times pokechecking has backfired on me. Checking feels super weightless and it just feels like a lol you can do is put bodies in front of the puck and hope you can get a check off with one of them. I can’t even check stationary players sometimes. My character just bounces off even with 45-60 checking. 

I’ll keep revisiting this game and will update my review if the controls improve. But right now I’m kinda disappointed.

Love the idea, dislike the execution.
Mainly because the AI has the equivalent of "rubberbanding" in racing games... Basically, if you starting playing too well or winning too much, the AI will cheat (unlimited sprint, perfect aim, perfect tackles, etc) to catch-up to you or put the challenge back up.

Player-side AI all over is terrible. Your players will not check at all unless you get an upgrade that makes them prioritize checking. Check hitboxes are really narrow/wonky, while enemies have very generous hitboxes.

The really damning part is the game will forcibly change which player you are controlling frequently, and commonly at unintuitive moments. The pass button is also hard-bound to the change player button, so if you want to change players and at the same moment one of your players obtains the puck, you will pass it off immediately.

A minor gripe, but one of the abilities is throwing that player's stick to knock some people down. Because you HAVE to control who has the puck and your teammates never use their abilities on their own, you cannot use this ability while maintaining control of the puck ever.

There's a fun game in here but currently it feels like the game is fighting you in places it shouldn't. I can probably recommend this after significant AI, controls, and player autonomy tweaks/overhauls, but I can't recommend it in its current state. It's just an exercise in frustration currently.

It's honestly mind-blowing to me that we can still get sports games like this in the 2020s, cheap and frustrating AI, half baked mechanics, and limited replay value.
First, the AI is way too unbalanced. You will dominate the game in shots on goal, time on attack, pass interceptions, and hits, and still somehow lose the game 2-1 or 3-0. The opponent goalie is way too strong, how many cross crease one-timers do I have to shoot in one possession, just for the AI to score on a lazy floater from the blue line that my goalie (whos usually in a bad position because the AI is terrible) helplessly watches fly past him? How many times do I have to poke check the opponent on defense until I can actually get the puck back? Why does the AI get frame-perfect body checks the moment one of your players touch the puck? If I had a quarter for every time the AI scored on a double tap deflect goal, I'd have enough money to hire a bigger dev team for this game. 
Your teammates are also another sore spot. They will go out of their way to make the game worse since the AI takes awful angles to loose pucks, rarely recovers defensive poke checks, and refuses to body check (more on this later) unless you put a powerup on them. Why are my teammates constantly skating towards me instead of taking a good offensive position to prepare for a pass? 
Speaking of passes... they are AWFUL. You can point your control stick or d-pad towards any teammate, and randomly your player will instead choose to fling the puck forward or at an opponent, ending your possession. The passing logic (if there is any) makes no sense, I've lost count on the amount of times I wanted to pass to the side and/or slightly behind me and the pass goes nowhere near where I aimed. This game could really use icon passing or some sort of improved logic. I don't know how many times I've said "I didn't aim my pass there!" when playing the campaign mode. 
The roguelike aspect of the game is okay, but it sometimes really hinders the hockey game underneath. Not being able to select any superstar teammate I want after I unlocked them is pretty crappy; I think choosing from a random pool of powerups can provide enough variability, but seeing the same 4 stars on rotation after I've unlocked all of them makes the game feel stale. When the run finally starts, I immediately feel a sense of dread looking at my benchwarmers since most of the time since their stats are abysmally low. Event spaces, while useful at times, are not often worth taking due to the potential downside most of the events give. It's much more useful to take a talent or raw stat boost over an event that sometimes provides a pure positive. 
I really REALLY want to give this game a chance, but I can't help but shake that weird feeling I get when I play any retro-like sports game with cheap AI. I don't want to get people the wrong idea though; for the casual couch co-op with friends (which is how I discovered the game), this game does enough to keep people entertained for a 40-60 minute session. Once you start to scratch a little further under the surface, however, the game's ugly underside really starts to show through.

As a retro hockey game, it works pretty well. Feels like an old Nintendo game. As a modern game with a meta structure for replayability, it falls pretty short. The game also feels like it wildly missed opportunities to embrace it's theme. 

It just feels very shallow. I realize it's still early access, so maybe there's a lot more coming, but there just isn't that much going on past the core gameplay. There's only about 4 skills unlocked with about 4 more you can buy, but even they don't feel terribly different. Hit the puck off your opponent's face or hit it off your teammate's face, the end result is pretty indistinguishable. Let me start off by saying that I enjoy this game a lot. It has simple enough hockey echanics that let you do fun and wacky stuff on the ice. The only thing is that if you are going to have simple mechanics, you have to REALLY nail them, and this game does not. 

This may be a bit of a longer review so TLDR: character targetting sucks, events are bad, and expert mode feels like a enemy team stat boost on top of smarter AI

Ok, lets start with mechanics. The two mechanics that I really have a problem with are the targetting on changing character (this includes passing) and the aiming of where the goalie throws the puck after they catch it. Both of these feel awful enough consistently for me to say multiple times a game “that is NOT where I pointed my joystick.” Then I think maybe I actually did, and when I go to run my joystic around its housing, I find that I was actually pointing where I wanted, the game just decided it wasn't that direction. This is terrible when you want to pass to 1 of 2 people that are near each other, and passing to the wrong one means an interception, which gets more punishing in expert mode as I will talk about later. When your goalie has the puck, you can aim directly to either side, and there will just be a chance you throw it backward, into your goal possibly. Why am i throwing the puck like 5° behind my player and into my net. That should not even be possible. If I am aiming there, just have me throw it a bit out so that I can not score on myself. This wouldn't be as much of a problem if it passed correctly out of the goalie though. 

Next, I want to talk about why the design of the events in this game are garbage. EVERY event that I have come across has a negative. I understand that there may be an even that doesn't have one, but I know that there are some that just only have negatives. If you have the chance of an only positive event being even 1/10, I will ALWAYS just go and rest or train or get a talent, all of which are either a pure stat positive, or make the gameplay more interesting and dynamic. If the player tries events and gets anevent that is ≤=neutral a handful of times before the get a positive one, they will just avoid events. 

Now on to expert mode. First off, standard mode is right where it should be, with enough of a challenge to be interesting, but easy enough to win your 2nd or 3rd run. Now, when you go up to standard mode, not only does the opponent ai (further referred to as npcs for sake of simplicity) get a stat boost (very noticeable from their benchwarmers having better accuracy and shot power than what seems like most of my star players) but they also just have a way smarter ai. This combo scales the difficulty almost exponentially instead of linearly, as in it seems like going from difficulty 2 to 4 instead of 2 to 3 (or more accurately 3 to 9 instead of 3 to 4). On top of the start boosts and just being smarter, it seems as if their range for intercepting gets increased. This is a problems by itself, but paired with the bad targetting the game becomes a game where you cannot make a single mistake or it is just an instant goal. And when you know that this mistake wasn't your fault but that of the poor targetting system, you get tilted, and start making more mistakes yourself.

These game design mistakes make the game on expert mode just feel suffocating and straight up unfair, instead of an increased challenge to an already fun game.
